title: Optimization under quality floors
task_statement: Cut cost and latency only while the quality floor and the safety guard still hold. (Inference: wording from secondary sources)

components.name: Batch processing for work that can wait
components.first_principle: Work that no user waits for can trade latency for a lower token price.
steps: Send work that no user waits for to the Batch API.
Keep interactive requests on the synchronous Messages API.
Check the batch status before you read the results.
Read the results after all requests finish or after 24 hours.
Score the results against the quality floor before you change production. (Inference)
Resubmit expired requests in a new batch. (Inference)
pros: Batch pricing gives 50 percent off each token.
The discount also applies to cached tokens in a batch.
Results stay available for 29 days, so the team can review them later.
cons: Results can take up to 24 hours.
Managed Agents sessions cannot use batch processing.
Batch requests wait in a queue with their own rate limits.
use_when: Evaluation runs, backfills, and scheduled jobs can wait for results.
A nightly grader pass runs over the eval set.
The team can accept results up to 24 hours after submission.
do_not_use_when: A user waits for the answer in the product.
The workflow needs an interactive Managed Agents session.
A request sets max_tokens to 0 for a cache warm-up, which batches do not support.

constraints.choice: Send every unattended request through the batch interface.
constraints.combination: Combine the batch discount with prompt caching for shared prefixes.

constraints.choice: Accept a result window of up to 24 hours.
constraints.combination: Use the synchronous path for any request a user waits for.

constraints.choice: Keep each batch below 100,000 requests and 256 MB.
constraints.combination: Split a larger job into several batches. (Inference)

constraints.choice: Read the results within 29 days of batch creation.
constraints.combination: Store results in your own system when you need them later. (Inference)

constraints.choice: Plan for the Batches API rate limits, which are shared across all models.

components.exam_tie: D4.5. Expect a scenario with a large unattended job and a cost limit. The credited answer uses the batch interface and keeps calls that users see synchronous. (Inference)
components.trap: Streaming a nightly job to cut its latency. Streaming changes the timing of the first token, and the job still pays the synchronous price.
components.decision_rule: Send unattended work to the batch interface, and keep any request a user waits for synchronous.
components.exam_tip: A job with a deadline of minutes does not fit batch processing.

components.name: Model tier and effort choice
components.first_principle: The cheapest model and effort that clear the quality floor give the lowest cost per completed task.
steps: Measure the quality floor on the eval set for each candidate model and effort.
Pick the cheapest model and effort that clear the floor.
Compare the candidates on cost per completed task.
Route only the task types that the cheaper tier handles above the floor.
Re-run failed tasks at a higher effort when outcomes are checkable.
Audit prompts after each model change.
pros: A smaller tier can cut latency and cost on tasks it handles well.
Effort is one control for speed and cost on Claude Haiku 5.5.
Routing lets easy tasks skip the costlier tier.
cons: A cheaper tier can fail the quality floor on hard tasks.
Routing rules need upkeep when the task mix changes. (Inference)
Each tier needs its own prompt audit after a change. (Inference)
use_when: Speed or cost binds and the quality floor is known.
Tasks differ in difficulty in a way the input shows. (Inference)
A time-sensitive workflow can use the fastest tier that passes the floor.
do_not_use_when: No eval floor exists yet, so the comparison has no line. (Inference)
All tasks are hard and only the strongest tier clears the floor. (Inference)

constraints.choice: Choose a faster tier and a lower effort for time-sensitive work.
constraints.combination: Stream the response to show the first tokens early.

constraints.choice: Compare candidates on cost per completed task.
constraints.combination: Report the floor result for each route next to the cost. (Inference)

constraints.choice: Audit prompts against the model after each model change.
Route by task type, not by user identity. (Inference)
Assign one person to own the routing rule and its eval results. (Inference)

components.exam_tie: D4.5. Expect a scenario with a latency target above the limit and a quality floor near its line. The credited answer measures each stage and changes one lever at a time. (Inference)
components.trap: Routing all traffic to the cheapest tier. The cost falls, but hard tasks fail the quality floor.
components.decision_rule: Choose the cheapest model and effort that clear the quality floor on each task route.
components.exam_tip: A speed gain is valid only when the quality floor still holds after the change.

decision_flow:
flowchart TD
  A{User waits for the answer?} -->|Yes| B[Synchronous Messages API]
  A -->|No| C{Result can wait up to 24 hours?}
  C -->|No| D[Synchronous Messages API]
  C -->|Yes| E[Batch API at 50 percent of token price]
  E --> F{Quality floor holds on a sample?}
  F -->|No| G[Use a stronger tier or higher effort]
  F -->|Yes| H[Ship the cheaper route]
cheatsheet:
flowchart LR
  W[Unattended work] --> B[Batch API]
  B --> D[50 percent off tokens]
  B --> L[Up to 100k requests or 256 MB]
  B --> X[Results up to 24 hours]
  U[User waits] --> S[Messages API]
  T[Easy tasks] --> C[Cheaper tier]
  H[Hard tasks] --> R[Stronger tier or effort]

patterns.rule: Measure each stage, then cut the lever with the least quality cost first. Check the floor after each cut.

patterns.answer_type: routing with a floor per route

traps: Route everything to the cheapest tier
